stories.headline: All election guarantees fulfilled, says Arvind Kejriwal; Opposition slams AAP of misusing public resources
stories.title: All election guarantees fulfilled, says Arvind Kejriwal; Opposition slams AAP of misusing public resources
stories.summary: The Opposition parties accuse AAP of misusing Punjab’s public resources to organise a party event while the State grapples with a mounting financial crisis
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Ahead of the Assembly elections in Punjab, due in early 2027, Aam Aadmi Party’s national convener Arvind Kejriwal on Thursday (November 26, 2026) urged women to persuade the men in their families to vote for the AAP.

He was speaking at a rally in Moga on the party’s foundation day, where he highlighted the ₹1,000 financial assistance provided by the AAP Government to help women deal with inflation, taking a dig at the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) Government at the Centre.
The Opposition parties, meanwhile, targeted the AAP, accusing it of misusing Punjab’s public resources to organise a party event while the State grapples with a mounting financial crisis.

Mr. Kejriwal claimed that the AAP had fulfilled all its election guarantees within five years, adding that the Congress, the Shiromani Akali Dal and the BJP had announced that they would discontinue the AAP Government’s existing schemes if voted to power.
“I am standing before people of Punjab today because my ‘Chota Bhai’, Chief Minister Bhagwant Singh Mann, has fulfilled all of Kejriwal’s guarantees.
We promised free electricity and people are getting free electricity.
We promised to organise ‘tirth yatra,’ and now devotees are going on the ‘yatra.’ We promised to open Aam Aadmi Clinics and now people are receiving great treatment.
We promised free treatment, and everyone has been provided with a health insurance card worth ₹10 lakh,” he said.
The Smart Ration Card Scheme to extend food security benefits to 10 lakh beneficiaries was also launched at the event.

Leader of the Opposition in the Punjab Assembly Partap Singh Bajwa alleged that the Government machinery, including State-owned buses, administrative resources and police personnel were deployed for a political function at the expense of the public exchequer.
“Before calling it a ‘Khushhaal Rally’, the AAP must answer a fundamental question: has Punjab actually become prosperous under its rule?
When the State is drowning in debt, why is public money being spent on a party celebration?

stories.headline: Antibiotic resistance threat grows in Kashmir
stories.title: Antibiotic resistance threat grows in Kashmir
stories.summary: Expert calls for tighter curbs on sale of high-end antibiotics outside hospitals Uniform antibiotic policy urged across healthcare institutions ‘Most winter infections are viral, don’t require antibiotics’ Srinagar, Nov 26: Rampant misuse, self-medication and indiscriminate prescriptions are fuelling antibiotic resistance in Kashmir, raising concerns that life-saving drugs could become ineffective against common infections. Experts have called for urgent regulatory measures and responsible antibiotic use to tackle the growing threat. Every year, World Antimicrobial Resistance Awareness Week (WAAW) is observed from November 18 to 24 to raise awareness about antimicrobial resistance (AMR), with concerns mounting over easy over-the-counter access to antibiotics and gaps in prescription enforcement. Dr Syed Mudasir Qadri, Additional Professor, Department of Internal and Pulmonary Medicine, SKIMS, described the ever-increasing antimicrobial resistance as a ‘silent pandemic’ that requires urgent attention. “It is going on unabated, and if corrective measures are not taken well in time, we may end up with no antibiotics to treat us and our future generations,” he said. Qadri said people need to understand that not every infection requires systemic antibiotics, including oral, intravenous or intramuscular drugs, particularly when the infection is not caused by bacteria. He said the ongoing transition from autumn to winter, marked by falling temperatures and dry air, makes people more vulnerable to viral infections, many of which do not require antibiotic treatment. “The majority of these infections don't need antibiotic therapy, but people start self-medicating by taking over-the-counter antibiotics on their own,” he said. Qadri also expressed concern over the prescription of multiple or high-end antibiotics for simple infections that could be treated with first-line oral drugs. “There is a strong need to implement strict drug regulations on the availability of antibiotics, especially high-end parenteral antibiotics outside hospitals. Inside hospitals, we need to have permanently running Antimicrobial Stewardship Programmes (AMSP),” he said. Antimicrobial Stewardship is a structured programme aimed at combating AMR through the rational use of antibiotics. Qadri said the programme has been successfully running at SKIMS for the past eight years. Qadri said a uniform antibiotic policy is central to the programme and should initially be implemented across all PHCs, CHCs, district hospitals, GMCs and other healthcare institutions. At a later stage, he said, these measures could also be extended to the private healthcare sector. “A uniform antibiotic policy is like a guideline that all doctors follow for the treatment of infections, whether it is empirical therapy, definitive therapy or even prophylactic therapy,” he said. Qadri said such a policy could significantly help reduce antibiotic resistance and improve culture positivity rates, as observed at SKIMS following the implementation of its Antimicrobial Stewardship Programme. He also stressed the importance of preventing infections to reduce antibiotic consumption. “The other important step to reduce antibiotic consumption is prevention of infections. This can be achieved by following the usual principles of cleanliness, eating healthy food, keeping yourself warm in winters, following your doctor's advice and, of course, vaccination whenever and wherever prescribed by your doctor,” he said. Highlighting the challenges in developing new antibiotics, Qadri said the first antibiotic, penicillin, was discovered accidentally by Alexander Fleming in 1928. He said no new class of antibiotics has been introduced into the market since 1987, a period often referred to as the 'discovery void'. “Developing a new antibiotic is a huge task even in this era of huge technological advancement. It takes years and sometimes decades to get a new antibiotic into the market for human use. On top of this, rampant and inappropriate use of antibiotics has led to the emergence of resistance to a wide variety of antibiotics, rendering them useless for treating infections,” he said. Doctors warn that the growing use of antibiotics also exposes patients to adverse effects and places an additional financial burden on individuals, hospitals and the public healthcare system due to the high cost of treatment. Qadri said antibiotics should be avoided for viral illnesses such as the common cold and flu, which are prevalent during the winter season. “Majority of infections are viral in origin and do not require antibiotics. People need to be aware and responsible and not fall into the trap of using antibiotics when just paracetamol or other symptomatic treatment may be enough,” he said. He said the irrational use of antibiotics was a serious public health concern requiring stronger policy interventions and effective enforcement at the national level. The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), in a report last year, also warned that antibiotics were increasingly proving ineffective against common infections such as pneumonia and urinary tract infections (UTIs), largely due to their indiscriminate and irrational use, highlighting the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance.

stories.headline: SC cracks whip on banks over prosecution of officials in homebuyer fraud cases
stories.title: SC cracks whip on banks over prosecution of officials in homebuyer fraud cases
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has demanded that HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Sammaan Capital, and PNB Home Finance provide unconditional sanctions. These sanctions involve officials implicated in collusion with builders in housing fraud schemes. The banks' CMDs must articulate their non-compliance in court if not met within a week. CBI’s investigations have led to chargesheets, and trials will commence once the necessary sanctions are secured, underscoring the urgency for timely judicial processes.

stories.headline: Central team assesses monsoon damage in Doda, Kishtwar
stories.title: Central team assesses monsoon damage in Doda, Kishtwar
stories.summary: Doda/Kishtwar, Nov 26: An Inter-Ministerial Central Team (IMCT) has assessed damage to critical infrastructure caused by cloudbursts, flash floods and landslides during Monsoon-2026 in Doda and Kishtwar districts, reviewing restoration and relief measures undertaken by the respective district administrations. The team, led by Gaya Prasad, Joint Secretary (F-II), Ministry of Home Affairs, comprised Shyam Kejriwal, Chief Engineer (DP&M), Ministry of Power, Central Electricity Authority; Prabhat Kumar, Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Rural Development; and Shachi Jain, Director, Central Water Commission, Ministry of Jal Shakti. In Doda, the team visited flood- and landslide-affected areas of Thathri and assessed the damage to public infrastructure and essential services. It also held a meeting with Deputy Commissioner Krishan Lal, who briefed the members on the impact of heavy rainfall, flash floods and landslides, including damage to roads, bridges, power infrastructure and water supply schemes. The team reviewed restoration and rehabilitation works and was apprised of the challenges faced in restoring connectivity and essential services in remote and hilly areas. The district administration also briefed the members on relief efforts and disaster preparedness measures. In Kishtwar, the team met Deputy Commissioner Pankaj Kumar Sharma, who presented details of damage to public infrastructure and private property, besides outlining relief, restoration and rehabilitation measures. The team also visited cloudburst-affected areas in Chatroo, inspecting three sites, including Dugga, Guzar-Gurinal Link Road and the Helipad Road to Guzar via Tehsil Complex. It assessed damage to roads, water supply schemes and other essential facilities and reviewed ongoing restoration works. The assessment is aimed at evaluating the extent of monsoon-related losses and reviewing the requirements for restoration and rehabilitation in the affected districts.

stories.headline: SC seeks census SOPs from Centre, Directorate of Census Operations
stories.title: SC seeks census SOPs from Centre, Directorate of Census Operations
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday asked the Centre and the Directorate of Census Operations to place on record the standard operating procedures governing the conduct of the census within a week. This would include the methodology and safeguards for recording and verifying caste-related information. A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana took note of the submission made by Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre, that she would apprise the court of the relevant SOPs. The bench asked the law officer to provide the details within a week. In its order dated October 12, the bench had requested the solicitor general to place on record the census SOPs being followed. It also directed that a complete set of the paper book be provided to the advocate-on-record for the Centre and the office of the solicitor general. A plea by Aakash Goel raised concerns over the methodology and safeguards for collecting and verifying

stories.headline: Supreme Court sets four-month deadline for FSSAI to finalise stricter food labelling norms
stories.title: Supreme Court sets four-month deadline for FSSAI to finalise stricter food labelling norms
stories.summary: The court has asked FSSAI to treat ‘total sugars’ and ‘saturated fat’, rather than ‘added sugar’ and ‘added fat’, alongside salt, as the nutrients of concern
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Observing that the right to health casts an obligation on the state to regulate industry practices detrimental to public health, the Supreme Court on Thursday (November 26, 2026) directed the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to formulate a single-phase front-of-pack nutrition labelling (FoPNL) regime mandating prominent red warning labels on packaged foods high in sugar, saturated fat or salt.
The court also asked the regulator to “strictly adhere” to the four-month deadline for finalising the draft regulations.

The judgment is the culmination of a series of interventions by a Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran in a public interest litigation (PIL) filed by the Kerala-based NGO 3S and Our Health Society seeking mandatory front-of-pack warning labels on packaged foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fat.

“The population’s exposure to harmful substances must be controlled, their consumption must be discouraged, and consumers must be protected from practices detrimental to health used by the food businesses.
Preventive measures that are most effective must therefore be undertaken in an effort to respect, protect and guarantee the right to health,” the Bench said.

In a direction that will require the FSSAI to recalibrate the thresholds for mandatory warning labels, the Bench asked the regulator to treat “total sugars” and “saturated fat”, rather than “added sugar” and “added fat”, alongside salt, as the nutrients of concern, in keeping with the regulatory consensus that preceded the 2024 Dietary Guidelines for Indians (DGI).
The Bench cautioned that the thresholds must be neither too high nor too low.

Excessively high thresholds, it said, would allow unhealthy products to escape scrutiny, leaving consumers unknowingly exposed to harmful levels of sugar, saturated fat and salt, while excessively low thresholds could result in nearly all packaged foods carrying warnings, eventually desensitising consumers and inducing “label fatigue”.

The court also prescribed changes to the design of the warning labels, directing the FSSAI to provide a separate red hexagon for each nutrient of concern, with a standardised pictorial representation accompanied by the words “HIGH FAT”, “HIGH SUGAR” or “HIGH SALT”.
Products exceeding the thresholds for multiple nutrients would thus have to carry distinct warnings for each.
Drawing on international practices, the Bench directed that each hexagon occupy a minimum of 4% to 5% of the package’s principal display panel, unless reasons exist for departing from this standard.

“The FSSAI shall also prescribe the font size of the text within each hexagon such that it is prominent, conspicuous and readily legible to consumers when viewed together with the pictorial representation of each nutrient-of-concern under normal conditions of purchase and use,” the Bench said.

stories.summary: In a move reflecting ongoing tensions, the Indian Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has urged Netflix to limit access to Pakistani content, particularly an upcoming series set to debut on December 4. This action follows previous advisories related to national security concerns amid the India-Pakistan conflict. Netflix has not clarified the series' availability in India, as industry groups pursue legal actions against Pakistani media.

stories.title: Kashmir tourism arrivals surpass 2025 tally
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 26: Kashmir’s tourism industry has shown signs of recovery in 2026, with tourist arrivals during the first seven months of the year surpassing the total recorded throughout 2025, according to a research paper published by Dr Sajad Ahmad Mir. The study, titled Tourism Industry in Kashmir, India: A Secondary-Data Analysis of Tourist Flows, Economic Contribution, Resilience and Sustainability Challenges, states that the Valley received 12.45 lakh tourists between January and July 2026, marking a 49.6 per cent increase compared with the corresponding period last year. The recovery comes after a sharp decline in tourist arrivals following the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam attack, which was followed by military tension and floods. According to the paper, Kashmir recorded 29.87 lakh tourist arrivals in 2024, its highest-ever figure. However, arrivals fell by 62.6 per cent to 11.16 lakh in 2025. The study found that tourism in Kashmir remains highly vulnerable to disruptions, with visitor confidence playing a major role in determining the industry's performance. It also highlighted the sector's economic importance, stating that tourism contributes approximately seven per cent to Jammu and Kashmir's Gross State Domestic Product and supports around five lakh livelihoods, directly and indirectly. The paper noted that more than 97 per cent of tourist arrivals since 2021 have been domestic visitors, while foreign tourist numbers have remained comparatively low. Foreign arrivals in 2025 were still 30.3 per cent below their 2019 level. The study also pointed to the growing homestay sector, with registered homestays increasing from 1,485 to 2,350, reflecting expanding accommodation capacity and opportunities for local communities. However, it cautioned that increasing accommodation facilities alone would not ensure stability unless tourist arrivals and the tourism season also expanded. The researcher recommended a comprehensive crisis-management plan, promotion of new destinations, development of tourism products beyond the summer and winter seasons, and stronger efforts to attract foreign visitors. The paper also called for reliable tourism statistics, improved facilities and greater participation of local communities in tourism-related activities. It concluded that Kashmir's tourism industry has demonstrated a strong capacity to recover, but sustainable growth will depend on visitor confidence, diversification and preparedness for future disruptions.
